articles.title: OHF calls for protection against smart-home lock-in
articles.dek: Its choice paper asks for local control, documented interfaces and limits on removing features after purchase.
body: The Open Home Foundation calls for smart-home products to keep working locally when cut off from the internet, and for manufacturers to document the interfaces needed to connect them to other systems. Its new choice position paper treats interoperability as a way for households to choose devices, materials and controls that suit their own needs.

The paper asks lawmakers to protect the ability to extend products without the original manufacturer’s permission. It also calls for restrictions on removing basic functionality after purchase, with exceptions for specific security risks and technical problems that cannot reasonably be solved. These are policy recommendations, not newly enacted protections.

The foundation includes its own field in the proposals: certification programmes should benefit users without imposing arbitrary access restrictions or pay-to-play barriers. It also argues that open systems should let people choose closed products, pairing deep customization with accessible defaults.

pullRequests.title: Add choice position paper and update documents section

articles.title: Home Assistant adds exceptions to broad automation targets
articles.dek: Exceptions stay in place as rooms, floors and labels gain new devices.
body: Home Assistant lets an automation target a whole room, floor or label while leaving selected entities, devices or areas out. The exclusions are resolved each time the automation runs, so adding a light to an excluded room does not accidentally bring it into the action.

The target picker gains an Exclude button and shows how many entities each exception removes. Checkboxes in the target details offer another way to refine the selection, while exclusions that no longer affect anything appear separately for cleanup.

Jan-Philipp Benecke supplies the matching controls and backend. The work implements the public opportunity shaped by Niels and Marcin Bauer; Niels reports the related implementation complete and reopens the discussion for feedback while its status remains Building. Excluding a group removes the group entity itself, not its individual members.

articles.title: Home Assistant adds a Talk control for compatible cameras
articles.dek: A Labs preview starts with supported Reolink cameras and requires a microphone-capable connection.
body: Home Assistant adds two-way audio to its camera viewer, letting someone watching a compatible camera speak through its speaker. The Talk control starts a new WebRTC stream with a return audio channel; Reolink supplies the first integration support for cameras using RTSP.

The feature is an opt-in Labs preview. In a browser, microphone access requires HTTPS. Matching iPhone app support carries microphone audio through a native connection when the page uses ordinary HTTP; Mac Catalyst is outside that app route. Cameras using Reolink’s RTMP or FLV streams do not receive the audio backchannel.
This extends Home Assistant’s own camera interface beyond viewing and snapshots. It does not establish talkback for the Matter cameras added to Home Assistant yesterday.

articles.title: Music Assistant preserves libraries when an upgrade fills the disk
articles.dek: A failed cleanup no longer erases the music library, and unfinished audio-analysis moves retry on later starts.
body: Music Assistant fixes an upgrade failure that could delete the entire music library when storage ran out. Moving audio-analysis data already stopped safely on a full disk, but a later cache cleanup failed too and triggered a recovery path that discarded the library database.

The cleanup failure now produces a warning without resetting the library. If the old analysis tables remain, each subsequent start checks for enough space and retries the move; without room, startup continues and reports the space needed. This prevents the loss rather than recovering a library already deleted.

articles.title: Community projects give old voice assistants a new purpose
articles.dek: A replacement Home Mini board raises more than sixteen times its crowdfunding goal, while Echo owners gain several ways to reuse their hardware.
body: An open replacement board for the first-generation Google Home Mini has raised $132,614 against an $8,000 crowdfunding goal, according to the Open Home Foundation’s October newsletter. Imre Laszlo’s MiciMike replaces the board inside an existing speaker, giving owners a route to Home Assistant voice control while keeping the enclosure.

The newsletter also highlights distinct paths for Amazon hardware: LocalDot replaces a third-generation Echo Dot’s mainboard, while EchoMuse turns a second-generation Dot into a local voice assistant and music player. TECHO5 repurposes an Echo Show as a Home Assistant voice satellite with a touchscreen.

These are device-specific community projects, rather than one upgrade for every old assistant. LocalDot is preparing a crowdfunding launch; the newsletter points readers to an Echo project comparison tool to match their hardware to the features they need.

externalSources.title: How to take back your voice

articles.title: ESPHome displays a browser dashboard on e-paper
articles.dek: A remote computer renders the page, while the panel receives its picture without running a browser.
body: ESPHome adds a way to show a browser dashboard on an e-paper or LCD panel. A computer runs the browser and shares its screen through VNC, a remote-screen protocol; the ESPHome device displays that picture. The component was tested on an M5Paper using the Home Assistant VNC web browser add-on.

Companion work compresses a dashboard screen from about one megabyte to tens of kilobytes and skips unchanged tiles. That prevents an e-paper display from refreshing needlessly whenever the remote browser repaints.

This first version is view-only and connects to servers that do not require a password. Password authentication and forwarding touchscreen input are separate follow-up work. Petar Petrov supplies the component and makes his first contribution to ESPHome’s documentation with its guide.

articles.title: Home Assistant opens settings tables to keyboard and screen-reader users
articles.dek: Rows, sorting controls and integration pages gain usable navigation and clearer names.
body: Home Assistant makes the shared settings tables usable without a mouse. The name in a clickable row becomes a keyboard-accessible button, and sortable column headings receive buttons that keep focus after changing the order.

Screen readers receive corrected row counts and named actions such as “Actions for Kitchen timer”. Integration pages gain clearer headings and control labels. Shared subpage navigation uses one keyboard stop per link instead of two, with a visible focus ring that survives high-contrast mode.

pullRequests.title: Make data tables usable with keyboard and screen reader
Improve screen reader support on the integrations dashboard
Tabs subpage improve tabs a11y

articles.title: Home Assistant makes chart ranges easier to explore
articles.dek: Drag-to-zoom and a shared history slider replace awkward chart-by-chart navigation.
body: Home Assistant charts with a time axis gain drag-to-zoom and a slider for moving or resizing the visible time range. The History page uses one floating zoom bar for all its charts, so a period of interest can be explored together.
On touch screens, dragging follows the tooltip instead of starting a zoom. Tapping a timeline marks the selected time, and a double tap or double click on the zoom slider returns to the full range.

Polish chart zoom on timelines and the zoom slider

articles.title: Home Assistant narrows troubleshooting logs to the affected integrations
articles.dek: Filtered views keep their search and log source in a bookmarkable link.
body: Home Assistant’s system logs gain an integration filter, letting someone troubleshooting a device read only the relevant integration’s messages. The condensed error list and live raw log follow the same selection, with existing messages and new arrivals kept in time order.

The selected log source, search and raw view stay in the URL, so a bookmark or reload returns to the same view. Browser Back restores the previous log source with its search, and new messages no longer collapse lines the reader already expanded.

articles.title: ESPHome removes passwords before sending logs across the network
articles.dek: Syslog messages stop carrying secrets that a terminal would merely hide.
body: ESPHome prevents its syslog connection from transmitting concealed secrets in plain text. When configured to forward the relevant logs, it previously sent values including Wi-Fi and MQTT passwords and WireGuard private keys to the log collector; terminal formatting only hid them visually.

The component replaces those values with “[redacted]” before building the outgoing message, regardless of its colour-stripping option. The correction addresses a finding from ESPHome’s 2026 security assessment.

pullRequests.title: [syslog] Redact LOG_SECRET values before sending a message

articles.title: Home Assistant stops iPhones appearing in several distant zones
articles.dek: A precise location stops inheriting a kilometre-wide accuracy radius from a mistaken arrival event.
body: Home Assistant’s iPhone app stops placing a person in several nearby zones after an unreliable region-arrival event. With Wi-Fi off, cellular positioning could report arrival for regions roughly a kilometre away; the app then widened an otherwise precise location reading to match.

The correction caps that widening at one hundred metres. A precise fix further outside the region is sent unchanged, instead of receiving an inflated radius that makes Home Assistant treat it as inside several places at once.

pullRequests.title: Stop widening location accuracy to reach far-away regions

articles.title: ESPHome controls Duco ventilation over a wired connection
articles.dek: Ventilation modes, comfort temperature and household air readings join the new component.
body: ESPHome adds a wired connection to Duco heat-recovery ventilation systems. It changes the ventilation mode and comfort temperature, and reads the ventilation level, remaining filter time and the time left in the selected mode.

The connection also reads temperatures, humidity and carbon dioxide from attached Duco sensors. Hardware testing covers a DucoBox Energy Comfort D325; support should not be assumed for every Duco system. Pieter Kokx supplies the component and guide in his first contributions to ESPHome and its documentation.

pullRequests.title: [duco] Component for Duco ventilation system
Documentation for Duco component

articles.title: Home Assistant reads BLUETTI Balco 260 power stations locally
articles.dek: A read-only connection supplies 45 sensors without relying on the manufacturer’s cloud.
body: Home Assistant adds a local connection for the BLUETTI Balco 260 power station, reading 45 sensors over Modbus TCP. The connection continues to work without the internet or BLUETTI’s cloud; this first integration does not change charging settings or write to the device.

Each poll checks the device’s serial number so a different unit at the same address cannot feed readings into the wrong history. Hardware testing covers the Balco 260; other models, expansion packs and writable controls remain outside this first implementation.

pullRequests.title: Add BLUETTI Modbus integration

articles.title: OHF keeps certification tied to devices as brands change hands
articles.dek: Shelly and Zooz face ownership changes; Works with Home Assistant still depends on meeting the programme’s requirements.
body: The Open Home Foundation says Jasco, Shelly and Zooz devices will retain Works with Home Assistant certification as long as they continue to meet the programme’s requirements. Its October newsletter addresses Schneider Electric’s planned takeover of Shelly early next year and Jasco’s acquisition of Zooz.

The foundation says its nonprofit structure keeps its own projects off the acquisition market. Its certification statement remains conditional on devices meeting the programme’s requirements; it does not guarantee every future product or business decision.

articles.title: Z-Wave JS rejects alarms claiming to come from another device
articles.dek: A device can no longer use an embedded address to impersonate a more securely connected node.
body: Z-Wave JS stops accepting an Alarm Sensor report as another device’s message solely because it names that device inside the report. Previously, even a node without a secure connection could inject an alarm attributed to another node and bypass that node’s security class.

The driver now drops a report when its embedded source identifies someone other than the sender, unless that source field is zero. Legitimately forwarded reports are also rejected because the forwarding cannot be verified.

pullRequests.title: fix: ignore Alarm Sensor reports forwarded on behalf of other nodes

articles.title: ESPHome switches can treat a power cut differently from a restart
articles.dek: A chosen startup state can coexist with keeping the current state through firmware updates.
body: ESPHome switches gain a way to turn on after power returns while keeping their previous state through a restart or wireless firmware update. Makers choose a starting state and storage that survives a software restart but loses its remembered state when power is removed.

This suits a connected load whose supply is also controlled by a wall switch or power strip. A Sonoff S31 test kept its off state through restarts and an update, then turned on after a power cut. Existing restore-mode configurations remain supported.

articles.title: Home Assistant’s Linux installer hides internal eMMC from removable drives
articles.dek: An unmounted internal disk no longer appears as an SD card ready to erase.
body: Home Assistant’s installer stops listing internal eMMC storage as a removable SD card on Linux. The running system’s disk was already protected, but an unmounted internal disk containing another installation could still appear in the drive chooser.

The installer reads the kernel’s device type to distinguish SD cards from eMMC. If the type cannot be read, it hides the device; older removable MMC cards are hidden too. The change has automated Linux coverage but has not been checked on real eMMC hardware.

articles.title: Home Assistant asks what is not working throughout November
articles.dek: The next What the heck month will invite feedback from users and the people they live with.
body: The Open Home Foundation announces November as its next month of What the heck, asking people what is not working well in their smart homes. Its invitation includes the people they live with, broadening the feedback beyond the person who set up Home Assistant. The October newsletter says further details are still to come.
